1	# michi — Overview
2	> orin-axi · Draft · June 2026
3	
4	---
5	
6	## What it is
7	
8	`michi` is a Rust crate of pure agentic response primitives — the formatting
9	and signalling conventions that make tools ergonomic for LLMs regardless of
10	protocol or language.
11	
12	It encodes six of the ten [AXI principles](https://axi.md) as typed, tested
13	Rust: TOON list rendering, key-value single-item rendering, contextual
14	disclosure (`help[]`), content truncation, definitive empty states, structured
15	errors with exit codes, idempotency signals, retry delay primitives, and
16	content-first status responses.
17	
18	The crate is intentionally narrow: **no protocol knowledge, no async runtime,
19	no CLI framework**. Pure computation — data in, strings and types out.
20	TypeScript consumers reach it via the NAPI npm wrapper `michi`. Rust
21	consumers take a direct crates.io or git dep.
22	
23	---
24	
25	## Name
26	
27	**michi** — from 道 (Japanese: path, way, road).
28	
29	The character 道 is the root of *dō* in martial arts and traditional arts:
30	judo, kendo, aikido, shodō, chadō. It means the path itself — and the act
31	of travelling it with intention. In the context of this crate, every `help[]`
32	block is michi: a marker that tells an agent which path to take next, with
33	what parameters.
34	
35	Fits the suite's naming aesthetic: short real words borrowed from a specific
36	domain, with a metaphor that earns its place.
37	
38	| Name | Origin | Meaning |
39	|---|---|---|
40	| Lumen | Latin | unit of luminous flux; light |
41	| Firkin | Middle English | small barrel; a measured unit |
42	| Monokl | Slavic / French | monocle; single-eye focus |
43	| Pulse | Latin | vital sign; rhythmic signal |
44	| **michi** | Japanese (道) | path, way, road |
45	
46	---
47	
48	## Organisation
49	
50	GitHub org: **orin-axi** (`github.com/orin-axi`)
51	
52	> "AXI" = Agent Experience Interface. The orin-axi org is the umbrella for
53	> tools designed to serve both human developers and AI agents as first-class
54	> users. `michi` is the primitive layer — the shared vocabulary of agent
55	> responses that all other tools in the suite can build on.
56	
57	---
58	
59	## Where michi fits in the suite
60	
61	```
62	orin-axi suite
63	  michi           ← this crate; AXI response primitives
64	                    imported by any agent-facing tool
65	  Monokl          ← AST-based semantic code search
66	                    uses michi for --format toon output
67	  Firkin          ← barrel file generator
68	                    uses michi for structured error output
69	  Lumen           ← coding session analysis + ambient context
70	                    uses michi for status + hint primitives
71	  Pulse           ← code health intelligence
72	                    uses michi for toon list output
73	```
74	
75	michi sits below every other tool in the suite as the shared primitive layer.
76	Non-agentic infrastructure tools (build scripts, formatters, etc.) never
77	encounter it — the package boundary enforces the separation.
78	
79	---
80	
81	## AXI principles encoded
82	
83	| Principle | Module | What it provides |
84	|---|---|---|
85	| P1 — TOON format | `toon` | Token-efficient list rendering (~40% vs JSON) |
86	| P2 — Minimal schemas | `kv` | Single-item KV rendering; field names appear once |
87	| P3 — Truncation | `truncate` | Size-bounded output with escape hatches |
88	| P4 — Aggregates | `toon`, `kv` | `totalCount` on every list/single-item response |
89	| P5 — Empty states | `empty` | Definitive `0 results` — never silent |
90	| P6 — Structured errors | `error` | `stdout` errors, typed exit codes, recovery hints |
91	| P7 — Ambient context | `status` | Content-first `StatusResponse` for no-arg invocations |
92	| P8 — Content first | `status` | `StatusResponse` — live state, not help text |
93	| P9 — Contextual disclosure | `hints` | `help[]` blocks with concrete next-step templates |
94	| Combined ops | `idempotency` | Already-done signals; partial success reporting |
95	
96	Not encoded (caller's responsibility): P10 (consistent `--help`), combined
97	operation design, tiered schema loading.

1	# axi-core — Specification
2	> Draft · June 2026
3	
4	---
5	
6	## Overview
7	
8	`axi-core` is a Rust crate of pure agentic response primitives — the
9	conventions that make tools ergonomic for LLMs regardless of protocol or
10	language. It is general-purpose: useful to anyone building AXI-compliant
11	tools, not tied to any specific stack.
12	
13	It encodes six of the ten [AXI principles](https://axi.md) as typed, tested
14	Rust: TOON list rendering, key-value single-item rendering, contextual
15	disclosure (`help[]`), content truncation, definitive empty states, structured
16	errors with exit codes, idempotency signals, retry delay primitives, and
17	content-first status responses.
18	
19	The crate has no protocol knowledge (no MCP, no HTTP, no CLI framework) and
20	no async runtime dependency. It is pure computation: data in, strings and types
21	out. TypeScript consumers reach it via the NAPI npm wrapper `axi-core`. Rust
22	consumers take a direct crates.io or git dep.
23	
24	---
25	
26	## Motivation
27	
28	AXI's 10 design principles describe how to build agent-ergonomic interfaces,
29	but the principles themselves are implemented ad-hoc — scattered as TypeScript
30	conventions in MCP servers, implicit CLI output patterns, and per-tool string
31	formatting. When `axi-core` exists:
32	
33	- The TOON format has a canonical, tested Rust implementation shared by both
34	  MCP and CLI consumers
35	- `help[]` hint construction, `totalCount` formatting, truncation signals, and
36	  recovery hint shapes are defined once and cannot drift between consumers
37	- Any agent-facing Rust CLI can import the same primitives directly
38	- Any TypeScript MCP server or CLI can reach them via the NAPI npm package
39	
40	A non-agentic tool (infrastructure CLIs, build scripts) uses its own output
41	conventions and never encounters axi-core. The package boundary enforces the
42	separation — agentic concepts do not leak into infrastructure.
43	
44	---
45	
46	## Non-goals
47	
48	- **Display-format Markdown** — research-grounded LLM display formatters
49	  (fields, sections, tables) are the caller's concern. axi-core is the
50	  `audience: ["assistant"]` compact surface; display rendering for the
51	  `audience: ["user"]` surface stays in your MCP SDK or application layer.
52	- **MCP protocol knowledge** — no `content[]`, no `outputSchema`, no
53	  `structuredContent`. Those are assembled by the calling MCP framework.
54	- **CLI framework** — no argument parsing, no stdin/stdout handling. That
55	  belongs to the caller's CLI framework of choice.
56	- **HTTP client** — no auth handling, no request construction. axi-core
57	  provides retry delay primitives that a caller plugs into their own HTTP
58	  client.
59	- **Async runtime** — zero tokio, zero async-std. All functions are sync
60	  and pure. Callers own retry loops and timeout semantics.
61	- **Full retry implementation** — axi-core provides `RetryConfig`,
62	  `parse_retry_after()`, and `next_retry_delay()`. The actual retry loop
63	  (sleep + re-execute) stays in the caller.
64	- **Caching** — callers should use `moka` or equivalent. axi-core does not
65	  include a cache.
66	- **Logging / telemetry** — Rust consumers use the `tracing` crate
67	  independently.
68	- **Schema validation** — input validation is the caller's concern.
69	- **MCP server bootstrapping** — `server.tool()`, tool discovery, deferred
70	  loading. Protocol-specific, stays in your MCP SDK.
71	
72	---
73	
74	## Consumer map
75	
76	```
77	Any Rust CLI binary
78	  Cargo.toml dep on axi-core (crates.io or git)
79	  Render --format toon via axi_core::render_toon()
80	  Full access to all modules — no NAPI overhead
81	
82	Any TypeScript CLI
83	  npm dep on axi-core
84	  --format toon dispatch calls into NAPI wrapper
85	  Same output; NAPI boundary is transparent
86	
87	Any TypeScript MCP server
88	  npm dep on axi-core
89	  Renders TOON for audience:["assistant"] content block
90	  Assembles MCP content[] from the returned string
91	```
92	
93	---
94	
95	## TOON format specification
96	
97	TOON (Token-Optimized Object Notation) is the agent-facing list format.
98	It front-loads structure (type, count, field names) so the LLM has full
99	context before reading any row, then encodes rows as compact comma-separated
100	values. Field names appear once in the header rather than once per row.
101	
102	**Why TOON for lists?**
103	Standard JSON repeats field names on every item. Markdown key-value format
104	repeats field names per item, which is ideal for single items and small sets
105	but expensive at scale. TOON trades per-item field repetition for a one-time
106	header, saving proportionally more tokens as N grows. For lists of 5+ items,
107	TOON is the better token budget choice. For single items or small metadata
108	blocks, key-value format remains preferred — see `kv::render_kv()`.
109	
110	AXI's benchmark shows this class of output optimization delivers approximately
111	40% token reduction over equivalent JSON for list data.
112	
113	### Grammar
114	
115	```
116	document     ::= type_header NEWLINE row+ totalcount? help_block?
117	type_header  ::= type_name "[" count "]" "{" field_list "}" ":"
118	type_name    ::= [a-z_][a-z0-9_]*                 (snake_case)
119	count        ::= [0-9]+                            (items in this response)
120	field_list   ::= field_name ("," field_name)*
121	field_name   ::= [a-z_][a-z0-9_]*
122	row          ::= "  " value ("," value)* NEWLINE   (2-space indent)
123	value        ::= scalar | quoted
124	scalar       ::= [^,\n"]*
125	quoted       ::= '"' ( [^"\\] | "\\" . )* '"'     (for values with commas)
126	totalcount   ::= "totalCount: " [0-9]+ NEWLINE     (total available, may exceed count)
127	help_block   ::= "help[" [0-9]+ "]:" NEWLINE hint+
128	hint         ::= "  " [^\n]+ NEWLINE
129	```
130	
131	### Examples
132	
133	**List response:**
134	```
135	issues[3]{number,title,state}:
136	  42,Fix login redirect,open
137	  43,Add dark mode,open
138	  44,"Update deps, bump major",closed
139	totalCount: 47
140	help[2]:
141	  Call get_issue with number=<number> for full detail
142	  Call list_issues with state=open to filter
143	```
144	
145	**Truncated field value:**
146	```
147	components[2]{name,description,tokens}:
148	  Button,"Primary action element (148 chars truncated — use full=true)",12
149	  Icon,"Scalable vector icon (203 chars truncated — use full=true)",8
150	totalCount: 84
151	help[1]:
152	  Call get_component with name=<name> and full=true for complete description
153	```
154	
155	**Empty state:**
156	```
157	issues[0]{}:
158	totalCount: 0
159	help[1]:
160	  Try list_issues with a broader filter
161	```
162	
163	**Single recovery hint (no list):**
164	```
165	help[1]:
166	  Retry create_item with suggestedParams: { project: "PROJ", type: "Task" }
167	```
168	
169	### Escaping rules
170	
171	- Values containing commas MUST be quoted
172	- Values containing double-quote characters use backslash escape: `\"`
173	- Values containing newlines MUST be truncated before rendering — TOON
174	  does not support multi-line cell values
175	- Null/absent values render as empty scalar: `val1,,val3`
176	- Boolean values: `true` / `false` literals
177	- Numeric values: rendered without quotes
178	
179	---
180	
181	## Rust public API
182	
183	### Crate root (`src/lib.rs`)
184	
185	```rust
186	pub mod toon;
187	pub mod kv;
188	pub mod hints;
189	pub mod truncate;
190	pub mod empty;
191	pub mod error;
192	pub mod idempotency;
193	pub mod resilience;
194	pub mod status;
195	pub mod response;
196	pub mod recovery;
197	
198	// Top-level re-exports for the common path
199	pub use hints::Hint;
200	pub use response::{AgentResponse, OutputFormat};
201	pub use toon::render_toon;
202	pub use kv::render_kv;
203	pub use error::{AxiError, ErrorCode};
204	pub use idempotency::{already_done, PartialSuccess, FailedOp};
205	pub use resilience::{RetryConfig, parse_retry_after, next_retry_delay};
206	pub use status::StatusResponse;
207	pub use truncate::{truncate, truncate_inline};
208	pub use empty::empty_state;
209	pub use recovery::RecoveryHint;
210	```
211	
212	---
213	
214	### `toon` — list rendering for N uniform-schema items
215	
216	TOON is the agent-facing format for lists. It front-loads structure (type,
217	count, field names) and encodes rows as compact comma-separated values.
218	Field names appear once in the header rather than once per row. Preferred
219	over key-value format for lists of 5+ items where token savings compound;
220	for single items, use `kv::render_kv()` instead.
221	
222	```rust
223	pub struct ToonOptions {
224	    /// Max cell value length before inline truncation.
225	    /// Appends "(N chars truncated — use full=true)" when exceeded.
226	    /// Default: 200
227	    pub max_cell_len: usize,
228	    /// Total items available. May exceed rows rendered.
229	    /// Emitted as "totalCount: N" line when Some.
230	    pub total_count: Option<u64>,
231	}
232	
233	impl Default for ToonOptions { ... }
234	
235	/// Render items as TOON.
236	/// Panics in debug if any row.len() != fields.len().
237	/// Returns empty-state TOON when items is empty.
238	pub fn render_toon(
239	    type_name: &str,
240	    items: &[Vec<Value>],
241	    fields: &[&str],
242	    hints: &[Hint],
243	    opts: ToonOptions,
244	) -> String
245	
246	pub enum Value {
247	    Str(String),
248	    Int(i64),
249	    Float(f64),
250	    Bool(bool),
251	    Null,
252	}
253	
254	impl From<&str>           for Value { ... }
255	impl From<String>         for Value { ... }
256	impl From<i64>            for Value { ... }
257	impl From<bool>           for Value { ... }
258	impl From<Option<String>> for Value { ... }
259	```
260	
261	---
262	
263	### `kv` — single-item key-value rendering
264	
265	Markdown key-value format for single items and small mixed-type metadata
266	sets. Benchmarks of LLM format retrieval accuracy show this format performs
267	strongly for single-item or small-N data where field name repetition is
268	acceptable. Column width is determined by the longest key.
269	
270	```rust
271	pub struct KvItem {
272	    pub key:   String,
273	    pub value: KvValue,
274	}
275	
276	pub enum KvValue {
277	    Text(String),
278	    Int(i64),
279	    Float(f64, u8),    // value, decimal places
280	    Bool(bool),
281	    Duration(std::time::Duration),
282	    Missing,           // renders as "—"
283	}
284	
285	/// Render key-value pairs with aligned columns.
286	/// Appends totalCount and help[] block when provided.
287	pub fn render_kv(
288	    items: &[KvItem],
289	    total_count: Option<u64>,
290	    hints: &[Hint],
291	) -> String
292	```
293	
294	Output for a single item:
295	```
296	name:         Button
297	variant:      primary
298	tokens:       12
299	description:  Primary action element
300	totalCount: 1
301	help[1]:
302	  Call list_components to see related
303	```
304	
305	---
306	
307	### `hints` — contextual disclosure blocks
308	
309	```rust
310	pub struct Hint(pub String);
311	
312	impl Hint {
313	    pub fn new(text: impl Into<String>) -> Self
314	}
315	
316	/// Render a standalone help[] block.
317	/// Returns empty string when hints is empty.
318	pub fn render_hints(hints: &[Hint]) -> String
319	
320	/// Append a help[] block to an existing body string.
321	/// Returns body unchanged when hints is empty.
322	pub fn append_hints(body: &str, hints: &[Hint]) -> String
323	```
324	
325	---
326	
327	### `truncate` — size-bounded output with escape hatches
328	
329	```rust
330	pub struct Truncated {
331	    pub content:      String,
332	    pub truncated:    bool,
333	    pub original_len: usize,
334	    /// "(N chars truncated — use full=true)" — None when not truncated
335	    pub signal:       Option<String>,
336	}
337	
338	/// Truncate content to at most `limit` chars.
339	pub fn truncate(content: &str, limit: usize) -> Truncated
340	
341	/// Truncate and append the signal inline.
342	/// Returns original string when it fits within limit.
343	pub fn truncate_inline(content: &str, limit: usize) -> String
344	```
345	
346	---
347	
348	### `empty` — definitive zero states
349	
350	```rust
351	/// Render an explicit empty-state TOON response.
352	/// Callers MUST use this — never return silent empty output.
353	///
354	/// Produces:
355	///   type_name[0]{}:
356	///   totalCount: 0
357	pub fn empty_state(type_name: &str) -> String
358	
359	/// Empty state with contextual hints.
360	pub fn empty_state_with_hints(type_name: &str, hints: &[Hint]) -> String
361	```
362	
363	---
364	
365	### `error` — structured errors with exit codes
366	
367	AXI P6: errors go to stdout (not stderr), carry exit codes, carry hints,
368	and never block on interactive prompts. `AxiError` encodes this as a type.
369	
370	The HTTP status → ErrorCode mapping is NOT in axi-core — callers produce
371	an `ErrorCode` after interpreting whatever failure occurred. This keeps the
372	module free of HTTP knowledge.
373	
374	```rust
375	pub struct AxiError {
376	    pub code:        ErrorCode,
377	    pub message:     String,
378	    pub hints:       Vec<Hint>,
379	    pub recovery:    Option<RecoveryHint>,
380	    pub retryable:   bool,
381	    pub retry_after: Option<std::time::Duration>,
382	}
383	
384	pub enum ErrorCode {
385	    // Non-retryable — agent should not retry without changing params
386	    InvalidInput,    // bad parameters
387	    NotFound,        // resource absent
388	    Unauthorized,    // auth failure
389	    Forbidden,       // permission denied
390	    Conflict,        // resource state mismatch
391	
392	    // Retryable — agent may retry same call
393	    RateLimited,     // 429 — check retry_after
394	    Unavailable,     // 503
395	    Timeout,         // request timed out
396	    ExternalFailure, // downstream error
397	}
398	
399	impl AxiError {
400	    pub fn new(code: ErrorCode, message: impl Into<String>) -> Self
401	    pub fn hint(mut self, hint: impl Into<String>) -> Self
402	    pub fn recovery(mut self, r: RecoveryHint) -> Self
403	    pub fn retry_after(mut self, d: std::time::Duration) -> Self
404	
405	    /// Render to stdout-ready string with hints attached.
406	    pub fn render(&self) -> String
407	
408	    /// AXI exit codes: 0 = success/already_done, 1 = all other errors.
409	    /// Callers should not invent additional codes.
410	    pub fn exit_code(&self) -> i32
411	}
412	```
413	
414	---
415	
416	### `idempotency` — already-done signals and partial success
417	
418	Provides types and rendering for idempotency checks, already-done detection,
419	and partial-success reporting. The caller owns the persistence layer that
420	tracks what has been done; axi-core provides the rendering contract.
421	
422	```rust
423	/// A canonical idempotency key.
424	pub struct IdempotencyKey(pub String);
425	
426	impl IdempotencyKey {
427	    /// Construct from operation name + a stable string representation of inputs.
428	    pub fn new(operation: &str, stable_input: &str) -> Self
429	    /// Construct from operation name + raw bytes (SHA-256 hashed).
430	    pub fn from_hash(operation: &str, data: &[u8]) -> Self
431	    pub fn as_str(&self) -> &str
432	}
433	
434	/// Render an already-done response.
435	/// Exits 0 — this is a successful no-op, not an error.
436	/// Produces a kv block with operation status + hints.
437	pub fn already_done(
438	    operation: &str,
439	    summary: &str,
440	    hints: &[Hint],
441	) -> String
442	
443	/// Partial success: some operations completed, some failed.
444	pub struct PartialSuccess {
445	    pub completed: Vec<String>,
446	    pub failed:    Vec<FailedOp>,
447	    pub skipped:   Vec<String>,
448	}
449	
450	pub struct FailedOp {
451	    pub operation: String,
452	    pub reason:    String,
453	    pub recovery:  Option<RecoveryHint>,
454	}
455

466	### `resilience` — retry delay primitives
467	
468	Pure computation only — no async, no network, no sleep. Callers build the
469	actual retry loop; axi-core provides the delay calculation and header
470	parsing.
471	
472	```rust
473	pub struct RetryConfig {
474	    pub max_attempts:   u32,                    // default: 3
475	    pub initial_delay:  std::time::Duration,    // default: 1s
476	    pub max_delay:      std::time::Duration,    // default: 30s
477	    pub backoff_factor: f64,                    // default: 2.0
478	    pub jitter:         bool,                   // default: true
479	}
480	
481	impl Default for RetryConfig { ... }
482	
483	/// Parse a Retry-After header value.
484	/// Accepts integer seconds ("120") or HTTP-date ("Wed, 21 Oct 2025 07:28:00 GMT").
485	/// Returns None for malformed or absent values.
486	pub fn parse_retry_after(value: &str) -> Option<std::time::Duration>
487	
488	/// Compute the next retry delay.
489	/// Applies exponential backoff, optional jitter, and clamps to max_delay.
490	/// Respects retry_after when provided — returns the larger of backoff and header.
491	pub fn next_retry_delay(
492	    attempt: u32,
493	    config: &RetryConfig,
494	    retry_after: Option<std::time::Duration>,
495	) -> std::time::Duration
496	
497	/// Whether a status code is conventionally retryable.
498	/// Returns true for: 429, 502, 503, 504.
499	pub fn is_retryable_status(status: u16) -> bool
500	```
501	
502	Usage pattern for a caller implementing their own retry loop:
503	```rust
504	let config = RetryConfig::default();
505	for attempt in 0..config.max_attempts {
506	    match call_api() {
507	        Ok(result) => return Ok(result),
508	        Err(e) if is_retryable_status(e.status) => {
509	            let retry_after = e.retry_after_header
510	                .and_then(|h| parse_retry_after(&h));
511	            let delay = next_retry_delay(attempt, &config, retry_after);
512	            sleep(delay).await;
513	        }
514	        Err(e) => return Err(e),
515	    }
516	}
517	```

727	## What this crate provides vs what stays in your application
728	
729	### Formalising conventions that are typically implicit
730	
731	| Concept | Where it usually lives | Provided as |
732	|---|---|---|
733	| Contextual hints after output | Implicit strings per tool | `hints::Hint`, `render_hints()`, `append_hints()` |
734	| Total count on list responses | Number passed ad-hoc | `ToonOptions::total_count`, `totalCount:` line |
735	| Recovery hints on failure | Ad-hoc per server/tool | `recovery::RecoveryHint`, `render_recovery()` |
736	| Retry delay calculation | Inside caller's retry loop | `resilience::next_retry_delay()` |
737	| Retry-After header parsing | Ad-hoc string parsing | `resilience::parse_retry_after()` |
738	| Retryable status classification | Hardcoded booleans per caller | `resilience::is_retryable_status()` |
739	| Error classification shape | Ad-hoc per tool | `error::AxiError`, `error::ErrorCode` |
740	| Empty state handling | Ad-hoc per tool (often silent) | `empty::empty_state()` |
741	| Truncation | Ad-hoc per tool, no standard signal | `truncate::truncate()`, `truncate_inline()` |
742	
743	### Genuinely new — does not exist as a shared primitive today
744	
745	| What | Why |
746	|---|---|
747	| TOON renderer | New format — token-efficient list encoding for agent context windows |
748	| `kv::render_kv()` | Single-item Markdown-KV with aligned columns; no standard Rust equivalent |
749	| `status::StatusResponse` | Typed P8 content-first orientation response — novel primitive |
750	| `idempotency::already_done()` | Typed already-done signal with canonical output format |
751	| `idempotency::PartialSuccess` | General partial-success reporting with per-op recovery hints |
752	| `idempotency::IdempotencyKey` | Canonical key construction with stable hashing |
753	| `AgentResponse` builder | Unified construction API across all consumers |
754	| NAPI wrapper | Cross-language bridge — TypeScript authors never write Rust |
755	| Formal TOON grammar | Canonical spec enabling interoperability and testability |
756	| `render_hints_only()` | Append hints to an existing body without re-rendering |

806	## Performance contract
807	
808	| Operation | Target | Basis |
809	|---|---|---|
810	| `render_toon()` — 100 items, 4 fields | < 500µs | Simple string allocation, no I/O |
811	| `render_toon()` — 1000 items, 4 fields | < 3ms | Linear in N×fields |
812	| `render_kv()` — 10 items | < 20µs | Column-width scan + string join |
813	| `render_hints()` — 5 hints | < 10µs | Trivial string join |
814	| `truncate_inline()` | < 5µs | Single pass, char boundary safe |
815	| `parse_retry_after()` | < 2µs | String parse only |
816	| `next_retry_delay()` | < 1µs | Pure arithmetic |
817	| NAPI boundary overhead | < 5µs | Established from napi-rs benchmarks |
818	
819	**Allocation:** `render_toon()` pre-allocates output capacity from
820	`items.len() × avg_row_estimate`. All functions are allocation-bounded —
821	no references held across call boundaries.
822	
823	**Thread safety:** All public functions are stateless pure functions.
824	`AgentResponse` is `Send + Sync`. NAPI wrapper uses napi-rs safe threading.
825	
826	Benchmarks via `criterion`. Run in CI on PRs touching `crates/axi-core/src/`.

937	## Open questions
938	
939	**Q1 — TOON vs Markdown-KV for agent-facing list responses**
940	AXI benchmarks the efficiency gains at the CLI/MCP level, but not the
941	downstream LLM retrieval accuracy of TOON vs Markdown-KV for list data.
942	Before treating TOON as universally superior for the `audience: ["assistant"]`
943	surface, run a retrieval accuracy experiment: same list data, TOON vs
944	Markdown-KV, retrieval task, across a few model sizes. If Markdown-KV wins
945	on retrieval accuracy despite higher token cost, the right call for MCP
946	consumers may be to use Markdown-KV even for lists. The crate ships either
947	way — the question is which format callers should default to.
948	
949	**Q2 — External Rust consumer strategy**
950	For external Rust binaries to depend on `axi-core`, options:
951	(a) crates.io publish — cleanest for public consumers once API is stable
952	(b) git dep with tag: `axi-core = { git = "...", tag = "v0.x.y" }` — good
953	    for early adopters before crates.io publish
954	(c) private cargo registry — overhead not worth it
955	
956	Recommend (b) during development, (a) at first stable release. Gate
957	crates.io publish behind at least one real consumer integration test.
958	
959	**Q3 — `cli` feature scope**
960	Reserved for terminal-aware rendering. If `--format toon` in a human
961	terminal context should wrap long rows or colourize the header, the `cli`
962	feature is where that lives. Out of scope for v1 — axi-core v1 targets
963	agent consumers only, not human-readable terminal output.
964	
965	**Q4 — `AgentResponse` builder vs standalone functions**
966	The spec proposes both: low-level functions (`render_toon()`, `render_hints()`)
967	and a high-level builder (`AgentResponse`). If the builder is the only
968	thing NAPI-exported, the low-level functions are Rust-only. If both are
969	exported, the NAPI surface grows. Recommend: export the builder and
970	`renderHints()`/`appendHints()` only — low-level functions are implementation
971	details available to Rust consumers.
972	
973	**Q5 — Recovery hint format**
974	The current spec uses `serde_json::Value` for param values — type information
975	is lost at the boundary. This is acceptable for display (agents read the
976	rendered string) but may not be acceptable if `structuredContent` in an
977	MCP context needs to carry typed recovery hints for client programmatic use.
978	If so, `RecoveryHint` needs a more precise type model. Confirm scope before
979	implementing.

983	## Supplement — implementation notes and design rationale
984	
985	### `AgentResponse` format routing
986	
987	The builder routes to TOON or KV based on which items method the caller uses,
988	not on item count. The caller is responsible for choosing the right format:
989	
990	```rust
991	// List of uniform-schema items → TOON
992	AgentResponse::new("issues")
993	    .items(rows, &["number", "title", "state"])   // → render_toon()
994	
995	// Single item or mixed-type metadata → KV
996	AgentResponse::new("issue")
997	    .kv_items(vec![
998	        KvItem { key: "number".into(), value: KvValue::Int(42) },
999	        KvItem { key: "title".into(),  value: KvValue::Text("Fix login".into()) },
1000	    ])                                             // → render_kv()
1001	```
1002	
1003	**Guidance:** use `.items()` when all rows share the same schema and there
1004	are 5 or more of them — TOON's token savings compound with N. Use
1005	`.kv_items()` for single items, mixed-type status data, or any case where
1006	the field names differ per row. A single-item `.items()` call works but
1007	produces a TOON header with one row, which is less readable and offers no
1008	token advantage over KV.
1009	
1010	---
1011	
1012	### `IdempotencyKey` — stable input serialisation
1013	
1014	`IdempotencyKey::from_hash(operation, data)` hashes the raw bytes of `data`.
1015	For the key to be canonical across calls with the same logical input, `data`
1016	must be produced deterministically:
1017	
1018	- **Maps and structs:** sort keys alphabetically before serialising to JSON.
1019	  `serde_json::to_vec` on a `HashMap` produces non-deterministic key order.
1020	  Use `BTreeMap` or a sorted intermediate representation.
1021	- **Floats:** avoid floating-point values in idempotency keys — representation
1022	  varies by architecture. Round to a fixed decimal or convert to integers.
1023	- **Timestamps:** exclude request-time fields (created_at, request_id) unless
1024	  the intent is a per-request key rather than a per-operation key.
1025	
1026	```rust
1027	// Correct: BTreeMap serialises with sorted keys
1028	let mut params: BTreeMap<&str, serde_json::Value> = BTreeMap::new();
1029	params.insert("project", json!("PROJ"));
1030	params.insert("type",    json!("Task"));
1031	let key = IdempotencyKey::from_hash("create_item", &serde_json::to_vec(&params)?);
1032	
1033	// Incorrect: HashMap key order is non-deterministic
1034	let params: HashMap<&str, _> = /* ... */;
1035	let key = IdempotencyKey::from_hash("create_item", &serde_json::to_vec(&params)?);
1036	// ^ same logical input may produce different keys on different calls
1037	```
1038	
1039	---
1040	
1041	### `is_retryable_status()` — why 500 is excluded
1042	
1043	The default retryable set is `{ 429, 502, 503, 504 }`. HTTP 500 (Internal
1044	Server Error) is intentionally absent.
1045	
1046	429 and 50x gateway errors (502, 503, 504) represent transient conditions —
1047	rate limits and upstream unavailability — where the same request is likely
1048	to succeed after a delay. 500 represents a server-side bug. Retrying a 500
1049	without changing anything about the request will produce the same 500. Worse,
1050	retrying write operations that returned 500 may produce duplicate side effects
1051	if the server processed the request before erroring.
1052	
1053	Callers that genuinely need to retry 500s (some APIs use it for transient
1054	conditions) can implement their own `is_retryable` predicate and pass it to
1055	their retry loop independently of `is_retryable_status()`.
1056	
1057	```rust
1058	// Default: 429, 502, 503, 504 only
1059	if is_retryable_status(status) { ... }
1060	
1061	// Custom: caller adds 500 for a specific API known to use it transiently
1062	let retryable = is_retryable_status(status) || status == 500;
1063	```
1064	
1065	---
1066	
1067	### `render_hints_only()` — the three-surface seam
1068	
1069	This method exists to support MCP frameworks that implement a three-surface
1070	response pattern: one content block for agent consumption
1071	(`audience: ["assistant"]`), one for display (`audience: ["user"]`), and a
1072	`structuredContent` payload for client tooling. In this pattern, the display
1073	body is rendered via the framework's own Markdown or rich-text layer, while
1074	the agent-facing block combines TOON output with a `help[]` trailer.
1075	
1076	Without `render_hints_only()`, framework code that has already rendered a
1077	display body would need to reconstruct an `AgentResponse` just to get a
1078	formatted `help[]` block to append to the agent surface.
1079	
1080	```typescript
1081	// Example: MCP framework TypeScript (simplified)
1082	function assembleToolResult(opts: RespondOpts): ToolResult {
1083	  const userBody      = renderDisplayMarkdown(opts.body);    // display surface → audience:["user"]
1084	  const hintsBlock    = axiCore.renderHintsOnly(opts.hints); // axi-core → append to assistant body
1085	  const assistantBody = opts.assistant                       // caller-provided TOON
1086	      ?? (userBody + "\n" + hintsBlock);                     // fallback: display body + hints
1087	
1088	  return {
1089	    content: [
1090	      { type: "text", text: assistantBody,
1091	        annotations: { audience: ["assistant"], priority: 1.0 } },
1092	      { type: "text", text: userBody,
1093	        annotations: { audience: ["user"],      priority: 0.5 } },
1094	    ],
1095	    structuredContent: opts.structured ?? null,
1096	  };
1097	}
1098	```
1099	
1100	`render_hints_only()` is the narrow seam between axi-core and the calling
1101	framework's rendering layer — it allows the `help[]` format to be owned by
1102	Rust without requiring the framework to understand TOON.
1103	
1104	---
1105	
1106	### `parse_retry_after()` — format details
1107	
1108	Accepts either of the two forms defined in RFC 7231 §7.1.3:
1109	
1110	| Form | Example | Notes |
1111	|---|---|---|
1112	| Integer seconds | `"120"` | Seconds to wait from response time |
1113	| HTTP-date | `"Wed, 21 Oct 2026 07:28:00 GMT"` | Absolute datetime, UTC only |
1114	
1115	Returns `None` for any malformed value — including valid HTTP-dates that are
1116	in the past. Callers should treat `None` as "use backoff only" and proceed
1117	with `next_retry_delay()` passing `retry_after: None`.
1118	
1119	Does not validate that an HTTP-date is in the future. If a server returns a
1120	past date (clock skew or bug), `parse_retry_after()` will return a zero or
1121	very small duration. `next_retry_delay()` internally clamps: the returned
1122	duration is always at least `config.initial_delay` and at most
1123	`config.max_delay`, regardless of what `parse_retry_after()` returns.
1124	
1125	```rust
1126	let retry_after = parse_retry_after(header_value);
1127	let delay = next_retry_delay(attempt, &config, retry_after);
1128	// next_retry_delay() already clamps to initial_delay minimum — no extra handling needed
1129	```
1130	
1131	---
1132	
1133	### `outputSchema` is in the LLM context
1134	
1135	A precision point that matters for token budget planning in MCP servers that
1136	use progressive disclosure or deferred tool loading:
1137	
1138	- **`outputSchema`** on a tool definition is part of the `tools/list` response.
1139	  It IS injected into the LLM context window at session start alongside
1140	  `inputSchema`. It adds schema tokens — roughly +15% on the schema component.
1141	  It is a one-time cost that amortises across the session as a prepaid
1142	  reasoning contract.
1143	
1144	- **`structuredContent`** in a tool result is client-consumed only. It does
1145	  NOT enter the LLM context window.
1146	
1147	This matters for deferred tool loading: adding `outputSchema` to tools that
1148	are not yet loaded would add schema tokens before those tools are called,
1149	defeating the purpose of deferral. `outputSchema` should only be defined on
1150	always-loaded tools, or it should be excluded from `tools/list` for deferred
1151	tools and supplied only when the tool is actually invoked.
1152	
1153	If your MCP framework auto-registers `outputSchema` from tool definitions,
1154	ensure it respects the deferred/always-loaded boundary when constructing
1155	`tools/list` responses.
1156	
1157	---
1158	
1159	### Build-time P4 — pre-computed aggregates at CI time
1160	
1161	AXI Principle 4 (pre-computed aggregates) is typically discussed as a runtime
1162	convention: always return `totalCount`, pre-filter before responding, emit
1163	summaries instead of raw data. But the same principle applies at build time,
1164	and that application is more powerful.
1165	
1166	**The pattern:** any deterministic computation that a tool needs repeatedly is
1167	a candidate for pre-computation in CI rather than per-request execution at
1168	runtime.
1169	
1170	**Canonical example: a build-time component index**
1171	
1172	Consider a design system component library. At build time, a bundler plugin
1173	can scan every component's definitions, resolve references, and write a static
1174	lookup index shipped with the MCP server package. When an agent calls
1175	`searchComponents()`, the handler reads from that static structure — no scanning,
1176	no resolution, no index construction per request.
1177	
1178	The agent pays zero turn cost for the computation. The CI pipeline pays it
1179	once. The result is faster responses, lower token cost per call, and no
1180	variance in response time.
1181	
1182	**When to apply it:**
1183	
1184	| Computation | Runtime | Build time |
1185	|---|---|---|
1186	| Filtering by user input | ✓ | — |
1187	| Counting available items | Runtime (`totalCount` field) | Build time (pre-count, embed in manifest) |
1188	| Resolving references between definitions | — | ✓ (bundler plugin) |
1189	| Indexing for search / BM25 | — | ✓ (write index to disk at build) |
1190	| Building dependency graphs | — | ✓ (static graph serialised to JSON) |
1191	| Generating tool output schemas | — | ✓ (schema library `toJsonSchema()` at registration) |
1192	
1193	Build-time P4 is a design decision, not a code pattern — it shows up during
1194	architecture planning, not implementation. Ask: "does this computation change
1195	per-request, or is it stable across many requests?" Stable computation belongs
1196	at build time.
1197

1	# michi — Overview
2	> orin-axi · Draft · June 2026
3	
4	---
5	
6	## What it is
7	
8	`michi` is a Rust crate of pure agentic response primitives — the formatting
9	and signalling conventions that make tools ergonomic for LLMs regardless of
10	protocol or language.
11	
12	It encodes six of the ten [AXI principles](https://axi.md) as typed, tested
13	Rust: TOON list rendering, key-value single-item rendering, contextual
14	disclosure (`help[]`), content truncation, definitive empty states, structured
15	errors with exit codes, idempotency signals, retry delay primitives, and
16	content-first status responses.
17	
18	The crate is intentionally narrow: **no protocol knowledge, no async runtime,
19	no CLI framework**. Pure computation — data in, strings and types out.
20	TypeScript consumers reach it via the NAPI npm wrapper `michi`. Rust
21	consumers take a direct crates.io or git dep.
22	
23	---
24	
25	## Name
26	
27	**michi** — from 道 (Japanese: path, way, road).
28	
29	The character 道 is the root of *dō* in martial arts and traditional arts:
30	judo, kendo, aikido, shodō, chadō. It means the path itself — and the act
31	of travelling it with intention. In the context of this crate, every `help[]`
32	block is michi: a marker that tells an agent which path to take next, with
33	what parameters.
34	
35	Fits the suite's naming aesthetic: short real words borrowed from a specific
36	domain, with a metaphor that earns its place.
37	
38	| Name | Origin | Meaning |
39	|---|---|---|
40	| Lumen | Latin | unit of luminous flux; light |
41	| Firkin | Middle English | small barrel; a measured unit |
42	| Monokl | Slavic / French | monocle; single-eye focus |
43	| Pulse | Latin | vital sign; rhythmic signal |
44	| **michi** | Japanese (道) | path, way, road |
45	
46	---
47	
48	## Organisation
49	
50	GitHub org: **orin-axi** (`github.com/orin-axi`)
51	
52	> "AXI" = Agent Experience Interface. The orin-axi org is the umbrella for
53	> tools designed to serve both human developers and AI agents as first-class
54	> users. `michi` is the primitive layer — the shared vocabulary of agent
55	> responses that all other tools in the suite can build on.
56	
57	---
58	
59	## Where michi fits in the suite
60	
61	```
62	orin-axi suite
63	  michi           ← this crate; AXI response primitives
64	                    imported by any agent-facing tool
65	  Monokl          ← AST-based semantic code search
66	                    uses michi for --format toon output
67	  Firkin          ← barrel file generator
68	                    uses michi for structured error output
69	  Lumen           ← coding session analysis + ambient context
70	                    uses michi for status + hint primitives
71	  Pulse           ← code health intelligence
72	                    uses michi for toon list output
73	```
74	
75	michi sits below every other tool in the suite as the shared primitive layer.
76	Non-agentic infrastructure tools (build scripts, formatters, etc.) never
77	encounter it — the package boundary enforces the separation.
78	
79	---
80	
81	## AXI principles encoded
82	
83	| Principle | Module | What it provides |
84	|---|---|---|
85	| P1 — TOON format | `toon` | Token-efficient list rendering (~40% vs JSON) |
86	| P2 — Minimal schemas | `kv` | Single-item KV rendering; field names appear once |
87	| P3 — Truncation | `truncate` | Size-bounded output with escape hatches |
88	| P4 — Aggregates | `toon`, `kv` | `totalCount` on every list/single-item response |
89	| P5 — Empty states | `empty` | Definitive `0 results` — never silent |
90	| P6 — Structured errors | `error` | `stdout` errors, typed exit codes, recovery hints |
91	| P7 — Ambient context | `status` | Content-first `StatusResponse` for no-arg invocations |
92	| P8 — Content first | `status` | `StatusResponse` — live state, not help text |
93	| P9 — Contextual disclosure | `hints` | `help[]` blocks with concrete next-step templates |
94	| Combined ops | `idempotency` | Already-done signals; partial success reporting |
95	
96	Not encoded (caller's responsibility): P10 (consistent `--help`), combined
97	operation design, tiered schema loading.
98	
99	---
100	
101	## Namespaces
102	
103	| Surface | Name |
104	|---|---|
105	| Rust crate (crates.io) | `michi` |
106	| npm package | `michi` |
107	| Rust module path | `michi::` |
108	| GitHub repo | `orin-axi/michi` |
109	
110	---
111	
112	## License
113	
114	AGPL v3 (`AGPL-3.0-or-later`).
115	
116	Rationale: viral copyleft is well-suited to CLI/library tools embedded in
117	pipelines. Creates natural friction against agentic services wrapping michi
118	commercially without contributing back. A CLA or contributor copyright
119	assignment clause per repo preserves future dual-licensing optionality.
120	
121	---
122	
123	## Publishing targets
124	
125	- **crates.io** — public, `michi`
126	- **npmjs.com** — public, `michi` (NAPI wrapper)
127	- NAPI binaries cross-compiled via `cargo-zigbuild`:
128	  - `darwin-arm64`
129	  - `linux-x64-musl`
130	
131	---
132	
133	## Documents in this repo
134	
135	| File | Contents |
136	|---|---|
137	| `docs/00-overview.md` | This file — project identity, naming, suite context |
138	| `docs/01-spec.md` | Full technical specification — modules, API, grammar |
139	| `docs/projects/01-mvp.md` | MVP implementation plan — agent sessions, constraints |
140	
141	---
142	
143	## Open questions
144	
145	See `docs/01-spec.md` § Open questions for the five ADR items that need
146	resolution before or during the MVP build (TOON vs KV retrieval accuracy,
147	consumer strategy, `cli` feature scope, NAPI export surface, recovery hint
148	typing).

Base directory for this skill: /Users/gabe/.claude/plugins/cache/superpowers-marketplace/superpowers/5.1.0/skills/brainstorming

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you understand what you're building, present the design and get user approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until you have presented a design and the user has approved it. This applies to EVERY project regardless of perceived simplicity.
</HARD-GATE>

## Anti-Pattern: "This Is Too Simple To Need A Design"

Every project goes through this process. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config change — all of them. "Simple" projects are where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design can be short (a few sentences for truly simple projects), but you MUST present it and get approval.

## Checklist

You MUST create a task for each of these items and complete them in order:

1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer visual companion** (if topic will involve visual questions) — this is its own message, not combined with a clarifying question. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Visual questions ahead?" [shape=diamond];
    "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];

    "Explore project context" -> "Visual questions ahead?";
    "Visual questions ahead?" -> "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" [label="yes"];
    "Visual questions ahead?" -> "Ask clarifying questions" [label="no"];
    "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**The terminal state is invoking writing-plans.** Do NOT invoke frontend-design, mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. The ONLY skill you invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans.

## The Process

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Key Principles

- **One question at a time** - Don't overwhelm with multiple questions
- **Multiple choice preferred** - Easier to answer than open-ended when possible
- **YAGNI ruthlessly** - Remove unnecessary features from all designs
- **Explore alternatives** - Always propose 2-3 approaches before settling
- **Incremental validation** - Present design, get approval before moving on
- **Be flexible** - Go back and clarify when something doesn't make sense

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion:** When you anticipate that upcoming questions will involve visual content (mockups, layouts, diagrams), offer it once for consent:
> "Some of what we're working on might be easier to explain if I can show it to you in a web browser. I can put together mockups, diagrams, comparisons, and other visuals as we go. This feature is still new and can be token-intensive. Want to try it? (Requires opening a local URL)"

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Do not combine it with clarifying questions, context summaries, or any other content. The message should contain ONLY the offer above and nothing else. Wait for the user's response before continuing. If they decline, proceed with text-only brainstorming.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`

1	# michi — Specification
2	> orin-axi · Draft · June 2026
3	
4	---
5	
6	## Overview
7	
8	`michi` is a Rust crate of pure agentic response primitives — the
9	conventions that make tools ergonomic for LLMs regardless of protocol or
10	language. It is general-purpose: useful to anyone building AXI-compliant
11	tools, not tied to any specific stack.
12	
13	AXI (Agent eXperience Interface) is a set of ten design principles for
14	agent-ergonomic tooling that treats token budget as a first-class constraint.
15	Its thesis is that the "MCP vs. CLI" debate is the wrong frame: the real
16	question is which design principles make *any* interface effective for an LLM
17	agent. A well-designed interface following these principles measurably
18	outperforms both naive CLIs and MCP on task success rate, cost, duration, and
19	number of turns. `michi` encodes the subset of those principles that are pure,
20	language-agnostic computation — the parts that benefit from a single canonical,
21	tested implementation rather than ad-hoc re-derivation in every tool.
22	
23	It encodes **seven of the ten AXI principles** as typed, tested Rust: TOON
24	list rendering, key-value single-item rendering, contextual disclosure
25	(`help[]`), pre-computed aggregates (`totalCount`), content truncation,
26	definitive empty states, structured errors with exit codes, idempotency
27	signals, retry delay primitives, and content-first status responses.
28	
29	| AXI principle | michi module(s) |
30	|---|---|
31	| **P1 — Token-Efficient Output** | `toon`, `kv` |
32	| **P3 — Content Truncation** | `truncate` |
33	| **P4 — Pre-Computed Aggregates** | `ToonOptions::total_count` (the `totalCount:` line), `status` health summaries |
34	| **P5 — Definitive Empty States** | `empty` |
35	| **P6 — Structured Errors & Exit Codes** | `error`, `idempotency` |
36	| **P8 — Content First** | `status` |
37	| **P9 — Contextual Disclosure** | `hints`, `recovery` |
38	
39	The three remaining principles are deliberately out of scope: **P2 — Minimal

45	The crate has no protocol knowledge (no MCP, no HTTP, no CLI framework) and
46	no async runtime dependency. It is pure computation: data in, strings and types
47	out. TypeScript consumers reach it via the NAPI npm wrapper `michi`. Rust

content.text:
Good — got everything I need. oxc-react-codegen is the template. Here's the full synthesis across every area you raised:

---

## Crate selection: Rayon, miette, tokio?

**None of them belong in michi core.** Here's why:

- **Rayon** — parallelism for data-processing pipelines. michi has nothing to parallelize: `render_toon()` for 100 rows is <500µs, sequential, pure string building. Rayon would add a thread pool to a crate that does no I/O and holds no state.
- **miette** — beautiful human-readable diagnostic display. michi's errors (`AxiError`) are *agent-facing* — compact stdout strings, not terminal diagnostics. miette is for the human display surface michi explicitly excludes. Keep thiserror only.
- **tokio** (that's "taikio") — the spec says it explicitly: zero async. michi is pure sync. Callers own retry loops and sleep.

**What michi does need, derived from oxc patterns:**

| Dep | Why |
|---|---|
| `thiserror = "2"` | AxiError derives `std::error::Error` |
| `serde` + `serde_json = "1"` | RecoveryHint params, `render_json()` output |
| `sha2 = "^0.10"` | `IdempotencyKey::from_hash` — RustCrypto, zero transitive deps |
| `napi = "3"`, `napi-derive = "3"` | NAPI wrapper — **not v2, the spec is behind** |

Dev only:

| Dep | Why |
|---|---|
| `divan = "0.1"` | Benchmarks — **not criterion**, this is the current standard |
| `insta = { version = "1", features = ["yaml"] }` | Snapshot tests |
| `proptest = "1"` | Grammar conformance, truncation, retry |

---

## Lint, test, coverage, benchmarks

Straight from oxc-react-codegen's patterns:

**Test runner:** `cargo nextest` (parallel, faster, better output than `cargo test`). All CI test jobs use `taiki-e/install-action@nextest`.

## The AXI workflow insight

The thesis: agents are expensive at the turn level. Every back-and-forth costs context, latency, and money. An agent calling `get_pr`, then `get_checks`, then `get_comments`, then `analyze_diff` — four turns — is AXI anti-pattern. A single `review_pr` workflow tool that does all four internally and returns a synthesized response is one turn. **The leverage point is the workflow, not the individual operation.**

michi's current scope only helps with the *response format* of individual operations. It has no vocabulary for representing *workflow state* — multi-step progress, parallel step groups, compound results that synthesize multiple API calls.

---

## What this means architecturally

michi stays pure computation (no execution, no async, no I/O). But it should gain a **`pipeline` module** that provides the representation and rendering layer for workflow-level responses, exactly like how `resilience` gives you `next_retry_delay()` but not the retry loop.

The consumer executes the steps (possibly in parallel with rayon/tokio/whatever), then hands michi an assembled `Pipeline` to render. michi's job: canonical, compact, agent-readable output for multi-step state.

**Proposed `pipeline` module:**

```rust
pub struct Pipeline {
    pub name: String,
    pub steps: Vec<StepGroup>,   // groups allow parallel vs sequential modeling
    pub hints: Vec<Hint>,
}

pub struct StepGroup {
    pub mode: GroupMode,          // Sequential | Parallel
    pub steps: Vec<Step>,
}

pub enum GroupMode { Sequential, Parallel }

pub struct Step {
    pub name: String,
    pub status: StepStatus,
    pub summary: Option<String>,  // one-line result for compact view
    pub output: Option<String>,   // full TOON/KV blob (shown in verbose mode)
    pub error: Option<AxiError>,
}

pub enum StepStatus { Pending, Running, Done, Skipped, Failed }

impl Pipeline {
    pub fn new(name: impl Into<String>) -> Self
    pub fn step(mut self, step: Step) -> Self           // adds to sequential group
    pub fn parallel(mut self, steps: Vec<Step>) -> Self // adds a parallel group
    pub fn hint(mut self, hint: impl Into<String>) -> Self
    pub fn render(&self) -> String                      // compact TOON table
    pub fn render_verbose(&self) -> String              // includes per-step output blobs
    pub fn is_complete(&self) -> bool
    pub fn exit_code(&self) -> i32                      // 0 = all done/skipped, 1 = any failed
}
```

**The compact render format (TOON-compatible):**

```
pipeline[5]{step,status,summary}:
  validate_input,done,"Schema OK"
  fetch_pr,done,"PR #42 — 3 files changed"
  fetch_checks,done,"3/3 passing"
  post_review,failed,"Unauthorized — check token scope"
  notify_team,skipped,""
progress: 3 done · 1 failed · 1 skipped
help[1]:
  Retry post_review after fixing token scope — all prior steps already complete
```

This is standard TOON with `pipeline` as the type name, plus a `progress:` summary line — one new line type in the grammar.

**Parallel group render:**

```
pipeline[6]{step,status,summary}:
  [parallel]
  fetch_pr,done,"PR #42"
  fetch_checks,done,"3/3 passing"
  fetch_diff,done,"847 lines changed"
  [sequential]
  analyze,done,"2 potential issues found"
  post_comment,pending,""
  request_review,pending,""
progress: 4/6
```

The `[parallel]` / `[sequential]` group headers are new grammar productions that agents learn to parse.

## One thing I want to validate before writing the design doc

The `progress:` line and `[parallel]` / `[sequential]` group headers are **new grammar productions** in TOON. That's a meaningful spec extension — agents trained on TOON without pipeline context won't know the group header syntax.

Two options:

**A) Extend the TOON grammar** — `[parallel]` / `[sequential]` become first-class productions. Clean, but every parser (including any test-only parsers) needs updating. Agents need to handle unknown header lines gracefully.

**B) Encode groups in the type name** — `pipeline_parallel[3]{...}:` and `pipeline_seq[3]{...}:` as separate TOON blocks within one response, separated by blank lines. Backward-compatible with the existing grammar — agents that don't know pipeline just see two TOON blocks.

I lean **B** — simpler for agents, no grammar extension, works today. The group structure is implicit in the block ordering rather than explicit headers.

Strictly internal. The agent doesn't need to know *how* steps were executed — only what happened to each one.

From the agent's perspective, the grouping is irrelevant. It cares about:

- `post_review` failed
- `notify_team` was skipped
- What to do next

Whether `fetch_pr`, `fetch_checks`, and `fetch_diff` ran in parallel is the producer's implementation detail. The agent just sees three `done` rows.

So the rendered output stays flat TOON:

```

  fetch_pr,done,"PR #42 — 3 files changed"

  post_review,failed,"Unauthorized — check token scope"

  Retry post_review after fixing token scope — prior steps already complete
```

The `Pipeline` builder exposes `parallel()` and `step()` as an API convenience so the consumer can express *intent* — which is useful for the builder to determine dependency ordering (e.g. auto-skip steps that depend on a failed parallel group). That logic is internal. It never surfaces in the string output.

The only new grammar production is the `progress:` summary line — which is small, unambiguous, and parseable by any agent that encounters it cold.

No grammar extension needed, no `[parallel]` markers. Clean.

## The layer separation

```
Monokl / Firkin / Lumen / Pulse
         │
         ▼
  [execution crate]          ← this spec: tokio, moka, nucleo, surface adapters
  PipelineExecutor, Cache,
  FuzzyResolver, Resilience
         │  uses for rendering
         ▼

  AxiError, hints, recovery
```

michi stays exactly as specced — pure computation, zero tokio, zero moka. The execution crate depends on michi for formatting its output. When `McpSink::into_response_body()` needs to produce agent-readable step status, it uses `michi::Pipeline::render()`. When a step fails and needs an agent-readable error, it reaches for `michi::AxiError`.

This is the same pattern michi already models internally: `resilience.rs` gives you `next_retry_delay()` (pure computation); the execution crate's `with_resilience()` does the actual async loop using that delay value. Two distinct responsibilities, clear ownership.

## What this means for michi's `pipeline` module

The `pipeline` module I proposed for michi IS still needed — it's the typed rendering interface the execution crate builds against. But its scope is now precisely defined:

**In michi (pure data + rendering):**
```rust
pub struct Pipeline { name, steps, hints }
pub struct Step { name, status, summary, output, error }
pub enum StepStatus { Pending, Running, Done, Skipped, Failed }
impl Pipeline { fn render(&self) -> String }   // → TOON string
```

**In the execution crate (execution + results):**
```rust
pub struct PipelineResult { run_id, status, completed, failed, checkpoint }
pub struct PipelineExecutor { /* tokio-backed */ }
```

The execution crate converts its `PipelineResult` → michi's `Pipeline` → rendered string. The conversion is a thin adapter, not a deep coupling.

## The `AgentError` / `AxiError` question

The execution crate defines `AgentError` (HTTP, Timeout, Cancelled, etc.) and michi defines `AxiError` (InvalidInput, NotFound, RateLimited, etc.). These are parallel, not competing — they model different things:

- `AgentError` = what went wrong during execution (infrastructure perspective)
- `AxiError` = what to tell the agent (response formatting perspective)

The execution crate maps `AgentError → AxiError` when it needs to produce agent-readable output. That mapping lives in the execution crate, not in michi. Concretely:

```rust
// In execution crate — converts execution failure to michi agent output
fn to_axi_error(e: &AgentError) -> michi::AxiError {
    match e {
        AgentError::Http { status: 429, retry_after, .. } =>
            michi::AxiError::new(michi::ErrorCode::RateLimited, e.to_string())
                .retry_after(retry_after.unwrap_or(Duration::from_secs(60))),
        AgentError::Timeout { .. } =>
            michi::AxiError::new(michi::ErrorCode::Timeout, e.to_string()),
        // ...
    }
}
```

Clean boundary. Neither crate knows about the other's internals.

## Why one crate wins

**Feature flags give you the same guarantee as separate crates.** A consumer who just wants `render_toon()` adds `michi` with default features and pulls in zero tokio, zero moka, zero nucleo. The "pure computation" principle isn't enforced by convention — it's enforced by cargo:

```toml
[features]
default  = []                                           # pure sync, zero runtime
pipeline = ["dep:tokio", "dep:tokio-util",
            "dep:async-trait", "dep:uuid"]              # execution layer
fuzzy    = ["dep:nucleo-matcher", "pipeline"]           # fuzzy + pipeline
cache    = ["dep:moka", "pipeline"]                     # caching tier
cli      = ["dep:indicatif", "dep:inquire",
            "dep:crossterm", "dep:ctrlc", "pipeline"]   # CLI adapters
mcp      = ["pipeline"]                                 # MCP adapters (pure logic)
napi     = ["dep:napi", "dep:napi-derive"]              # npm wrapper
full     = ["pipeline", "fuzzy", "cache", "cli", "mcp"]
```

A Rust CLI that runs pipelines: `michi = { features = ["cli"] }`. An MCP server: `michi = { features = ["mcp"] }`. A tool that just formats output: `michi` with no features.

**The suite tools always want both.** Monokl, Firkin, Lumen, Pulse all need rendering primitives AND pipeline execution. Two crates means two deps, two version pins, two changelogs to track, two sets of breaking changes to coordinate. With one crate they write:

```toml
michi = { version = "0.1", features = ["cli"] }
```

That's the entire dependency story.

**Unified types eliminate the translation layer.** With two crates you need `AgentError → AxiError` conversions at the boundary. With one crate, there's one error type. The pipeline executor and the rendering functions live in the same type system — `michi::Error` carries both execution context and rendering semantics.

**One crates.io entry, one npm package.** External consumers discover one thing, version one thing, trust one API surface.

## The error type consolidation

One crate means one error type. The current spec has `AxiError` (michi, rendering-focused) and `AgentError` (execution spec, infrastructure-focused). In a unified crate these merge:

```rust
// src/error.rs
#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
pub enum Error {
    // Execution errors (pipeline feature)
    #[error("HTTP {status}: {message}")]
    Http { status: u16, message: String, retryable: bool, retry_after: Option<Duration> },
    #[error("Timeout after {elapsed:?}")]
    Timeout { elapsed: Duration },
    #[error("Cancelled")]
    Cancelled,
    // ... other AgentError variants

    // Domain errors (always)
    #[error("{0}")]
    InvalidInput(String),
    #[error("Not found: {0}")]
    NotFound(String),
    // ...
}

impl Error {
    pub fn render(&self) -> String { ... }   // agent-readable stdout string
    pub fn exit_code(&self) -> i32 { 1 }
    pub fn is_retryable(&self) -> bool { ... }
    pub fn class(&self) -> ErrorClass { ... }
}
```

`Sensitive<T>` stays. `ErrorClass` stays. The rendering methods (`render()`, `exit_code()`) live on the unified type so any error anywhere in the library can be formatted for agent consumption without a conversion step.

But this is a build artifact detail, not a conceptual split. `michi-node` is a thin shim that re-exports from the unified `michi` crate and wraps it for Node.

No. michi is too small to justify it.

Moon earns its place in large polyglot monorepos where you need affected-file task routing, cross-language dependency graphs, and aggressive caching across many projects. The value compounds with scale.

michi is two Cargo crates and a thin JS shim. The coordination problem Moon solves doesn't exist here:

- **Cargo** already handles the Rust workspace dependency graph
- **pnpm** (one `package.json` in `packages/michi-node`) handles the JS side
- **GitHub Actions** with `Swatinem/rust-cache` + pnpm's built-in cache handles CI speed

oxc-react-codegen has more JS complexity than michi (vite plugin, install matrix, multiple Node consumers) and doesn't use Moon.

Revisit if orin-axi ever consolidates Monokl, Firkin, Lumen, Pulse into a single monorepo — at that point Moon's affected detection and cross-project task graph would pay off. Not now.

Cargo + pnpm + Actions. That's the stack. Ready to write the design doc?

Yes to both. Here's how similar NAPI repos handle it and what fits michi.

---

## How other Rust + NAPI repos do it

Most follow one of two patterns:

**Pattern A — napi-rs template (npm package at root):** The repo root IS the npm package. Works for pure binding crates with no separate library. Not our shape — michi has a real Rust lib.

**Pattern B — workspace with binding subpackage (what we want):** Rust workspace at root, NAPI cdylib in a subdirectory. This is what oxc-react-codegen does, what SWC does, what Rolldown does. The binding is a build artifact of the library, not a peer.

---

## just + pnpm: yes

`just` is the single local interface across both Rust and JS. Developers run one tool regardless of which layer they're touching. pnpm handles the JS package in `packages/michi-node`. CI uses raw commands explicitly — just is for local ergonomics.

```justfile
# justfile

# List available recipes
default:
    @just --list

# ── Build ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

build:
    cargo build --workspace

build-release:
    cargo build --release --workspace

# Build the NAPI npm package (debug)
build-node:
    cd packages/michi-node && pnpm build --platform

# Build NAPI release binaries for publish
build-node-release:
    cd packages/michi-node && pnpm build --platform --release

# ── Test ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

test: test-rust test-node

test-rust:
    cargo nextest run --workspace

test-node: build-node
    cd packages/michi-node && pnpm test

# ── Lint ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

check: fmt-check clippy deny typos

fmt:
    cargo fmt --all

fmt-check:
    cargo fmt --all --check

clippy:
    cargo clippy --workspace -- -D warnings

deny:
    cargo deny check

typos:
    typos

# ── Snapshots ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

snapshots:
    cargo insta review

# ── Benchmarks ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

bench:
    cargo bench --workspace

# ── Coverage ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

coverage:
    cargo llvm-cov nextest --workspace --lcov --output-path lcov.info

# ── Full pre-push check ────────────────────────────────────────────────────

ci: check test bench
```

---

## pnpm workspace root — probably not

For v0.1 there's one JS package. A pnpm workspace root (`pnpm-workspace.yaml` + root `package.json`) adds ceremony for no gain right now. The justfile `cd`s into `packages/michi-node` for JS commands. Add the workspace root when a second JS package appears.

---

## Final repo shape

```
michi/
  Cargo.toml              ← [workspace] + [package] (michi lib)
  Cargo.lock
  rust-toolchain.toml     ← pinned stable toolchain
  build.rs                ← napi-build (feature-gated)
  justfile                ← task runner
  .rustfmt.toml
  .clippy.toml
  .typos.toml
  deny.toml
  CLAUDE.md
  README.md
  src/
    lib.rs
    toon/
    kv/
    hints.rs  truncate.rs  empty.rs  error.rs
    recovery.rs  status.rs  response.rs  idempotency.rs
    resilience/
    pipeline/
    fuzzy/       ← fuzzy feature
    cache/       ← cache feature
    sink/
    telemetry/
    adapters/
      cli/       ← cli feature
      mcp/       ← mcp feature
    napi.rs      ← napi feature
  benches/
    toon_render.rs
    kv_render.rs
  tests/
    toon_integration.rs
    kv_integration.rs
    resilience_integration.rs
    idempotency_integration.rs
    snapshot_tests.rs
  packages/
    michi-node/
      Cargo.toml           ← crate-type = ["cdylib"]
      package.json         ← name: "michi", published to npmjs
      index.js             ← platform loadBinding
      index.d.ts           ← generated by napi-derive
      src/lib.rs
      __test__/

  .github/

  docs/
    00-overview.md
    01-spec.md
    projects/
      01-mvp.md
      agents/              ← session briefs for S0–S4
```

---

That's the shape. One repo, one workspace, `just` as the local task runner, pnpm scoped to the node package. No Moon, no workspace root package.json yet.

5	
6	## Overview
7	
8	`michi` is a Rust crate of pure agentic response primitives — the
9	conventions that make tools ergonomic for LLMs regardless of protocol or
10	language. It is general-purpose: useful to anyone building AXI-compliant
11	tools, not tied to any specific stack.
12	
13	AXI (Agent eXperience Interface) is a set of ten design principles for
14	agent-ergonomic tooling that treats token budget as a first-class constraint.
15	Its thesis is that the "MCP vs. CLI" debate is the wrong frame: the real
16	question is which design principles make *any* interface effective for an LLM
17	agent. A well-designed interface following these principles measurably
18	outperforms both naive CLIs and MCP on task success rate, cost, duration, and
19	number of turns. `michi` encodes the subset of those principles that are pure,
20	language-agnostic computation — the parts that benefit from a single canonical,
21	tested implementation rather than ad-hoc re-derivation in every tool.
22	
23	It encodes **seven of the ten AXI principles** as typed, tested Rust: TOON
24	list rendering, key-value single-item rendering, contextual disclosure
25	(`help[]`), pre-computed aggregates (`totalCount`), content truncation,
26	definitive empty states, structured errors with exit codes, idempotency
27	signals, retry delay primitives, and content-first status responses.
28	
29	| AXI principle | michi module(s) |
30	|---|---|
31	| **P1 — Token-Efficient Output** | `toon`, `kv` |
32	| **P3 — Content Truncation** | `truncate` |
33	| **P4 — Pre-Computed Aggregates** | `ToonOptions::total_count` (the `totalCount:` line), `status` health summaries |
34	| **P5 — Definitive Empty States** | `empty` |
35	| **P6 — Structured Errors & Exit Codes** | `error`, `idempotency` |
36	| **P8 — Content First** | `status` |
37	| **P9 — Contextual Disclosure** | `hints`, `recovery` |
38	
39	The three remaining principles are deliberately out of scope: **P2 — Minimal
40	Default Schemas** is supported (callers pass exactly the fields they want) but
41	not enforced; **P7 — Ambient Context** and **P10 — Consistent Help** are
42	session-hook and CLI-framework concerns that live in the consuming tool, not in
43	a pure rendering crate.
44	
45	The crate has no protocol knowledge (no MCP, no HTTP, no CLI framework) and
46	no async runtime dependency. It is pure computation: data in, strings and types
47	out. TypeScript consumers reach it via the NAPI npm wrapper `michi`. Rust
48	consumers take a direct crates.io or git dep.
49	
50	---
51	
52	## Motivation
53	
54	AXI's ten design principles describe how to build agent-ergonomic interfaces,
55	but the principles themselves are typically implemented ad-hoc — scattered as
56	TypeScript conventions in MCP servers, implicit CLI output patterns, and
57	per-tool string formatting that drifts over time. When `michi` exists:
58	
59	- The TOON format has a canonical, tested Rust implementation shared by both
60	  MCP and CLI consumers
61	- `help[]` hint construction, `totalCount` formatting, truncation signals, and
62	  recovery hint shapes are defined once and cannot drift between consumers
63	- Any agent-facing Rust CLI can import the same primitives directly
64	- Any TypeScript MCP server or CLI can reach them via the NAPI npm package
65	
66	A non-agentic tool (infrastructure CLIs, build scripts) uses its own output
67	conventions and never encounters michi. The package boundary enforces the
68	separation — agentic concepts do not leak into infrastructure.

70	---

78	- **MCP protocol knowledge** — no `content[]`, no `outputSchema`, no
79	  `structuredContent`. Those are assembled by the calling MCP framework.
80	- **CLI framework** — no argument parsing, no stdin/stdout handling. That
